“The View” co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin, who was an aide to Donald Trump in his first term, likened the “eerie feeling” in the wake of major tech meltdowns to the weeks leading up to when COVID-19 upended daily life under the president.

“There is this eerie feeling that kind of reminds me of February of 2020, right before COVID hit, where it feels like something is about to go catastrophically wrong,” she said.

“I was there for COVID [in] 2020 — it was not a good response but there were actually very competent people in the first Trump administration. This one scares me because I don’t have confidence that there are any competent people.”

A wave of U.S. systems glitches have occurred recently, including the nationwide ground stop, disruptions to Microsoft programs, online access issues at major U.S. banks, a United Airlines system outage and, on Tuesday, an internal National Security Agency network reportedly going down.

Griffin slammed Trump officials over their public responses in recent days, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who used a Fox News hit on Monday to cite his talk with “one guy that’s very smart with tech” before speculating that artificial intelligence could be behind the outages.

“You are the secretary of homeland security,” she said. “Tech titans should be asking you what it is.”

Moments later, Griffin called out Vice President JD Vance who — when asked by Fox News’ Laura Ingraham on Monday about people stockpiling food and water — stated that “a lot” of his friends have reached out to him about preparing for a “crisis.” He then dismissed such concerns.

Elsewhere, in comments on the show’s “Behind the Table” podcast, Griffin stressed that there have been “more questions than answers” from the administration in the days since the nationwide ground stop.

“Because what I’m still struggling with is what was so serious in that moment that we had to ground a million passengers’ flights for hours that we were able to resolve in that amount of time and how do we have the confidence now that that patch or stop gap is solved and that all these flights are safe to fly?” she said.
